relevance.justification: All communication was strictly focused on task execution, ingredient gathering, and assembly coordination without any off-topic chatter.

clarity.justification: Messages were highly structured and unambiguous, explicitly stating robot identities, current locations, held items, and intended next steps.

grounding.justification: Agents frequently hallucinated holding items (e.g., R1 claimed to have the cooked meat patty at t=11s, R2 claimed to have the bun and tomato at t=10s), which directly led to failed ASSEMBLE and DROP actions later on.

coordination_utility.justification: Agents actively communicated about workstation locks to avoid deadlocks (e.g., R2 and R3 waiting for R1's lock to clear) and attempted to coordinate ingredient handoffs at the assembly table.

redundancy.justification: There was noticeable repetition, such as R1 repeatedly asking R2 to bring items (t=11s, t=12s) and R3 broadcasting very similar status updates while waiting at the assembly table (t=14s-17s).

planning_coherence.justification: Proposed plans correctly followed the recipe dependencies (cooking and cutting before assembly) and respected the need to gather all ingredients at one station, even though execution failed due to grounding issues.

failure_explanation_quality.justification: Agents clearly diagnosed failures, explicitly mentioning injected slips (t=4s), workstation locks (t=15s, t=18s), and missing inventory items (t=19s, t=25s), followed by logical recovery proposals.

llm_judge_report.overall_summary: The team communicated clearly and attempted to coordinate handoffs and manage locks effectively. However, severe hallucinations regarding their own inventory states led to a cascade of execution failures, despite logically sound planning and excellent failure reporting.
